screens.title: The Strategy Pattern: Interchangeable Algorithms
screens.narratorSegment: In this lesson we explore the Strategy pattern and why it matters when an object can perform the same task in several distinct ways. You will learn how to separate algorithm choices from the object that uses them so code stays small, testable, and open to extension. We will use concrete Java examples that show a shopping cart delegating discount calculations to pluggable strategy objects. Notice how this approach replaces large if-else or switch statements with small, focused classes. That makes each algorithm easier to test and maintain, and it supports the Open/Closed Principle because you can add new strategies without changing the context. As we move through the screens you will see the pattern components named clearly — Context, Strategy, and ConcreteStrategy — and see a runnable code walkthrough showing how to set and switch strategies at runtime. By the end you will be able to decide when Strategy simplifies a design, when it is overkill, and how it differs from the State pattern. Think about an e-commerce checkout where shipping or discounts vary by customer: how would you like to swap algorithms without editing the checkout logic?

screens.title: What is the Strategy pattern?
screens.narratorSegment: The Strategy pattern is a behavioral design pattern that defines a family of algorithms, encapsulates each algorithm in its own class, and makes them interchangeable within a context. In practical terms, the context delegates work to a strategy via a common interface and does not implement the algorithms itself. This separation keeps the context small and focused on coordination, while algorithm details live in dedicated classes that are easy to test. A concrete example is discount calculation: the ShoppingCart does not know how a particular discount is computed, it only asks its current DiscountStrategy to compute the final price. A key benefit is that you can add new strategies by creating new classes that implement the same interface, without changing the ShoppingCart; this supports the Open/Closed Principle. A common misconception is thinking Strategy is only about runtime swapping — while it enables that, its main value is encapsulation and clearer responsibilities. Consider a shipping calculation system: Strategy is ideal when multiple algorithms exist and you anticipate adding new ones or testing them in isolation. How would you design the interface for a task you need to swap?

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.5 › What is Strategy?
Pattern claim
The context delegates algorithm execution to a Strategy interface implemented by concrete classes.
Analogy
Think of a sorting toolbox: you pick quicksort, mergesort, or bubble sort as needed rather than reworking the caller each time.
When it shines
When a family of related algorithms exists and you need runtime flexibility or easier testing.
Misconception
Not always necessary for a single algorithm or tiny variations; it can add class overhead.
Definition cards
Context
Uses a Strategy reference and delegates algorithm execution to it. Does not implement the algorithm itself.
Strategy
An interface or abstract class declaring the method(s) the context calls.
Concrete Strategy
A class that implements the Strategy interface and provides a single algorithm variant.
Key Takeaway

Strategy moves algorithm code out of the context and into focused classes that are easy to extend and test.

screens.title: Core components: Context, Strategy, ConcreteStrategy
screens.narratorSegment: Let's examine the three core components and how they interact in a Java implementation. The Strategy interface declares the operation the context will call, such as applyDiscount or calculateCost. ConcreteStrategy classes implement that interface and encapsulate a specific algorithm; for example, NoDiscountStrategy returns the original price, PercentageDiscountStrategy reduces the price by a percentage, and FixedAmountDiscountStrategy subtracts a fixed amount. The Context, such as ShoppingCart, stores a reference to a Strategy and delegates execution to it. The Context may also provide a setter so clients can change the strategy at runtime. In practice this means the ShoppingCart's calculateFinalPrice method simply calls discountStrategy. applyDiscount(totalPrice) and returns the result. This separation reduces conditional branches in the Context and makes each algorithm independently testable. A common implementation pitfall is letting the Context inspect the type of strategy or use instanceof checks—this defeats the pattern. Instead, code to the Strategy interface and let the ConcreteStrategy implement the details. As you design these parts, also think about default strategies and how to inject them safely to avoid null references. Core components: Context, Strategy, ConcreteStrategy means strategy = interface; concretestrategy = algorithm implementation; context = delegates to strategy and supports runtime swapping.. In practical terms, roles and responsibilities in the java implementation. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

screens.title: Replacing conditional logic with Strategy
screens.narratorSegment: A frequent motivation for Strategy is replacing large conditional statements inside a class. Imagine a method filled with if-else branches to select multiple algorithms for shipping or discount calculations. Such code becomes brittle: adding a new algorithm requires editing the method, risking regressions and violating the Single Responsibility Principle. With Strategy, each algorithm is a separate class and the Context simply selects an instance to use. This yields several practical benefits: you can add a new ConcreteStrategy class without modifying the Context; unit tests can target each algorithm in isolation; and the Context logic stays short and readable. A common misunderstanding is that Strategy forces runtime selection. While it enables runtime choice, you can also choose a strategy once during construction and keep the Context unchanged afterwards. Another alternative is a factory method if the choice is made once at creation time. Use Strategy when algorithms form a family and you need flexibility or easier testing. Ask yourself: will algorithms likely grow or change? If yes, Strategy is a strong fit. Replacing conditional logic with Strategy means strategy reduces conditional complexity by moving algorithm selection into dedicated classes, improving testability and extensibility.. In practical terms, from if-else switches to pluggable algorithm classes. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Before: Conditional logic
One method branches on type or flags to decide which algorithm to run. Adding new options requires editing that method and retesting the whole class.
Drawbacks

  • Harder to unit test individual algorithms

Each algorithm is its own class implementing a common interface. The Context holds a reference and delegates the work, enabling extension by adding new classes only.
Benefits

  • Independent testing of algorithms

keyIdea.text: A concrete Java implementation shows how Context delegates to strategies and how swapping strategies changes behavior without editing the context.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.5 › DiscountStrategy Example
Code (abridged)
// 1. Strategy Interface
interface DiscountStrategy {
  double applyDiscount(double originalPrice);
}

// 2. Concrete Strategy: No Discount
class NoDiscountStrategy implements DiscountStrategy {
  @Override
  public double applyDiscount(double originalPrice) {
    System.out.println("Applying no discount.");
    return originalPrice;
  }
}

// 2. Concrete Strategy: Percentage Discount
class PercentageDiscountStrategy implements DiscountStrategy {
  private double percentage; // e.g., 0.10 for 10%

  public PercentageDiscountStrategy(double percentage) {
    this.percentage = percentage;
  }

  @Override
  public double applyDiscount(double originalPrice) {
    System.out.println("Applying " + (percentage * 100) + "% discount.");
    return originalPrice * (1 - percentage);
  }
}

// 2. Concrete Strategy: Fixed Amount Discount
class FixedAmountDiscountStrategy implements DiscountStrategy {
  private double fixedAmount;

  public FixedAmountDiscountStrategy(double fixedAmount) {
    this.fixedAmount = fixedAmount;
  }

  @Override
  public double applyDiscount(double originalPrice) {
    System.out.println("Applying fixed amount discount of $" + fixedAmount);
    return Math.max(0, originalPrice - fixedAmount);
  }
}

// 3. Context Class
class ShoppingCart {
  private DiscountStrategy discountStrategy;
  private double totalPrice;

  public ShoppingCart(double initialPrice) {
    this.totalPrice = initialPrice;
    this.discountStrategy = new NoDiscountStrategy();
  }

  public void setDiscountStrategy(DiscountStrategy discountStrategy) {
    this.discountStrategy = discountStrategy;
    System.out.println("Discount strategy set to: " + discountStrategy.getClass().getSimpleName());
  }

  public double calculateFinalPrice() {
    return discountStrategy.applyDiscount(totalPrice);
  }

  public void setTotalPrice(double totalPrice) { this.totalPrice = totalPrice; }
}
Example scenario
Create a ShoppingCart, set a PercentageDiscountStrategy, observe the reduced total, then switch to a FixedAmountDiscountStrategy without changing ShoppingCart code.
Explanation & guidance
  • Keep applyDiscount implementation details inside each strategy class.
  • Use a default strategy to avoid null checks in the Context.
  • Change strategies at runtime via a setter when client-driven selection is required.
Try this
Add a BuyOneGetOneFree strategy as an exercise. Keep ShoppingCart unchanged and test behavior.
Key Takeaway

The code shows how a small Context delegates large algorithm variations to focused Strategy classes that are easy to extend and test.

screens.title: Why Strategy supports Open/Closed and Testability
screens.narratorSegment: Here we make the practical case for using the Strategy pattern. The core claim is simple: when you move algorithmic variations into their own classes, your system becomes open for extension but closed for modification. That means adding a new algorithm rarely requires touching the context class or existing strategies. For example, if a ShoppingCart already delegates discounts to a DiscountStrategy interface, adding a seasonal discount only requires a new concrete class, not edits to the cart. This reduces risk and regression bugs when you extend behavior. You also gain testability: each concrete strategy has a narrow responsibility and can be unit-tested in isolation with simple inputs and expected outputs, without wiring a full ShoppingCart or UI. Reusability improves because multiple contexts can reuse the same strategy implementations where the algorithm applies. A common misunderstanding is that Strategy is only about avoiding switch statements; it is more about encapsulating variation and giving clients a clean way to choose algorithms at runtime. Finally, be mindful of cohesion: keep strategy classes focused and avoid moving unrelated responsibilities into them. Consider a quick reflective question: when you add a new algorithm, does any existing class change? If yes, Strategy might not yet be implemented correctly.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.5 › Benefits & Principles
Core Benefit

Open/Closed & Testability

Strategy isolates algorithm variants so new ones can be added without editing existing behavior. It also narrows responsibility for easier unit testing.

  • Easier to extend: add a ConcreteStrategy class.
  • Unit test each algorithm without the context.
  • Beware of over-splitting: avoid many tiny strategies with duplicated code.
Concrete Example
ShoppingCart Discounts

If ShoppingCart delegates to DiscountStrategy, adding a BuyOneGetOneFree strategy doesn't touch the cart code. That keeps the cart stable and makes strategy behavior testable independently.

When to use

Multiple variant algorithms that change independently or that clients select at runtime.

Common mistake

Creating strategies for tiny variations adds unnecessary complexity.

Architecture
Context (ShoppingCart)
Holds a DiscountStrategy reference and delegates calculation.
Strategy Interface
applyDiscount(originalPrice) — common contract.
Concrete Strategies
NoDiscount, PercentageDiscount, FixedAmount, BOGOStrategy
Key Takeaway

Use Strategy to keep the context stable and move variation into small, testable classes that can be added without changing existing code.

screens.title: Alternatives: Method Params, Factory, Template Method
screens.narratorSegment: Strategy is powerful, but it is not always the simplest solution. The key question to ask is: how many algorithms are there, and how likely are they to change or grow? If you have one algorithm with a small boolean variation, a method parameter is often clearer and faster to implement. For example, a sort method with an ascending flag does not need a family of strategy classes. A Factory Method is a lightweight alternative when the choice of algorithm is decided once at creation time and does not change at runtime — the factory returns the correct concrete object and the rest of the system uses it without switching strategies later. The Template Method pattern is another option when algorithms share structure and only differ in a few steps; in that case, a base class defines the skeleton and subclasses customise steps. A common error is defaulting to Strategy whenever polymorphism is needed; this can create class bloat when variations are tiny or unlikely to grow. Use the following simple decision heuristic: prefer a method parameter for minor or boolean toggles, Factory Method when the choice is fixed at creation, Template Method for shared structure with variant steps, and Strategy when you need runtime interchangeability and many independent algorithms. Ask yourself: will I add new behaviors often and require runtime switching? If yes, Strategy is the right fit.

Module 6 › Chapter 6.5 › Alternatives
Comparison

Strategy versus Simpler Patterns

Method Parameter

Best for small boolean or numeric switches. Minimal code, no extra classes.

Factory Method

Good when the decision is made at creation and does not change at runtime.

Template Method

Choose when algorithms share a common structure and vary in a few steps.

Decision Heuristic
  1. If differences are tiny, use a method parameter.
  2. If choice is fixed at creation, prefer a factory.
  3. If algorithms share steps, consider Template Method.
  4. If you need runtime interchangeability and many independent algorithms, use Strategy.
Pro Tip

Start simple. If you find your conditional logic growing and tests failing when you add cases, that is the sign to refactor to Strategy.

Common Mistake

Using Strategy for a single, stable algorithm creates unnecessary classes and complexity.

Quick Example

Use a parameter like sort(list, ascending) for a one-flag variation. Move to Strategy only when you need multiple independent sorting algorithms chosen at runtime.

screens.title: Strategy vs State: A Clear Distinction
screens.narratorSegment: Many learners confuse Strategy and State because both involve interchangeable objects that implement the same interface. The useful distinction is their intent. Strategy is about choosing an algorithm for a task, usually by the client: the context delegates to a strategy chosen by external code and the strategy does not typically change the context's identity. State is about changing the internal behavior of an object as its internal state changes; state objects may manage transitions and the object’s behavior evolves because of internal events. For instance, selecting a DiscountStrategy is a client decision: a checkout process or user input sets the discount policy. In contrast, a Document object might move through Draft, Review, and Published states, where the state objects change the document's behavior and may trigger transitions. A practical misconception is thinking both patterns should be used whenever you need polymorphic behavior; instead ask whether the choice is external and algorithmic (Strategy) or internal and lifecycle-driven (State). To test this, map who initiates the change: if the client chooses and swaps algorithms at runtime, that is Strategy. If the object’s own data causes behavior to change and transition, prefer State. Which one fits your scenario is the design decision you want to make consciously.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.5 › Strategy vs State
Definition Contrast
Strategy

Client chooses an algorithm. Context delegates to strategy; strategies are interchangeable and independent.

State

Object behavior changes with its internal state. States may alter transitions and behavior autonomously.

Example: Strategy

Checkout selects PercentageDiscountStrategy or FixedAmountStrategy based on a promotion code.

Example: State

An Order object moves from Pending to Shipped to Delivered and its allowed actions differ per state.

Misconceptions
  • They are interchangeable terms — they are not. Intent and who drives the change differ.
  • State objects often know about transitions; Strategy objects typically do not change the context’s state machine.
Reflection

Ask: who selects the behavior — the client or the object itself? Use that to guide your pattern choice.

keyIdea.title: Context Delegation
keyIdea.text: The PaymentProcessor delegates to a PaymentStrategy so different gateway implementations can be swapped without changing payment logic.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.5 › PaymentProcessor Walkthrough
Code Starter
// PaymentStrategy.java
interface PaymentStrategy {
  void pay(double amount);
}

// CreditCardPayment.java
class CreditCardPayment implements PaymentStrategy {
  private String cardNumber;
  public CreditCardPayment(String cardNumber) { this.cardNumber = cardNumber; }
  @Override
  public void pay(double amount) {
    System.out.println("Processing $" + amount + " with credit card " + cardNumber);
  }
}

// PaymentProcessor.java
class PaymentProcessor {
  private PaymentStrategy paymentStrategy;
  public PaymentProcessor(PaymentStrategy initial) { this.paymentStrategy = initial; }
  public void setPaymentStrategy(PaymentStrategy s) {
    this.paymentStrategy = s;
    System.out.println("Payment strategy set to: " + s.getClass().getSimpleName());
  }
  public void processPayment(double amount) {
    if (paymentStrategy == null) throw new IllegalStateException("No payment strategy set.");
    paymentStrategy.pay(amount);
  }
}
Testing Advice
  • Supply a fake or spy PaymentStrategy for unit tests to assert behavior without external APIs.
  • Keep retries and timeouts inside each concrete strategy, not in the processor.
  • Mock integration points for gateway-specific logic during integration tests.
Try This

Run the starter code, then call setPaymentStrategy with different implementations and observe console messages to see runtime swapping in action.

Key Takeaway

Keep the context simple. Let strategies hold external integration details and local error handling so behavior is modular and testable.

screens.title: Add, Test, and Maintain New Strategies
screens.narratorSegment: Follow a small, repeatable process when adding new strategies. Step one: design the strategy interface so it contains the minimal contract needed by the context. Step two: implement the new ConcreteStrategy focusing on a single responsibility; keep external integrations, logging, retries, and validation inside the strategy. Step three: write unit tests that exercise the strategy’s public method with representative inputs, edge cases, and error paths. Step four: integrate the new strategy into the system via dependency injection, a factory, or a configuration switch. Step five: perform an integration test with the context and a mock or sandbox endpoint to ensure interactions behave correctly. For example, to add a BuyOneGetOneFreeStrategy for the ShoppingCart, compute free items at the strategy level and return the adjusted price; then unit-test scenarios such as odd/even quantities and empty carts. A common mistake is changing the context to accommodate a new strategy; instead the context should remain unchanged. Maintainability tips: keep meaningful class names, document the algorithm’s assumptions, and add a short example test in the repository showing how to instantiate and exercise the strategy. This process keeps your system resilient as the set of algorithms grows.

keyIdea.title: Safe Extension Process
keyIdea.text: Design a minimal strategy contract, implement focused logic, unit-test thoroughly, integrate by injection, and avoid context changes.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.5 › Extending Strategies
Step-by-step
  1. Define the minimal interface contract required by the context and document preconditions.
  2. Implement a focused ConcreteStrategy that contains integration, logging, and error handling locally.
  3. Unit test the strategy in isolation with normal and edge cases; use fakes for external calls.
  4. Integrate via constructor injection, setter, or a factory so the context remains unchanged.
  5. Document the strategy with examples and add a small integration test with mocks or sandbox endpoints.
Example: BOGOStrategy

BOGO calculates free items and returns an adjusted total price. Unit tests should cover even and odd quantities, zero quantity, and price floor behavior.

Checklist
  • Single responsibility
  • Unit tests included
  • No context changes
  • Integration test or mock
Common Mistake

Placing validation or retry logic across multiple strategies instead of centralizing it when appropriate leads to inconsistent behavior.

Pro Tip

Keep strategies stateless where possible. If state is required, document lifecycle and avoid hidden side effects.

In this lesson we explore the Strategy pattern and why it matters when an object can perform the same task in several distinct ways. You will learn how to separate algorithm choices from the object that uses them so code stays small, testable, and open to extension. We will use concrete Java examples that show a shopping cart delegating discount calculations to pluggable strategy objects. Notice how this approach replaces large if-else or switch statements with small, focused classes. That makes each algorithm easier to test and maintain, and it supports the Open/Closed Principle because you can add new strategies without changing the context. As we move through the screens you will see the pattern components named clearly — Context, Strategy, and ConcreteStrategy — and see a runnable code walkthrough showing how to set and switch strategies at runtime. By the end you will be able to decide when Strategy simplifies a design, when it is overkill, and how it differs from the State pattern. Think about an e-commerce checkout where shipping or discounts vary by customer: how would you like to swap algorithms without editing the checkout logic?

By the end of these screens you will be able to explain what problem the Strategy pattern solves and implement it in Java. You will learn to design a context that accepts a strategy interface, build concrete strategy classes for each algorithm variant, and switch strategies at runtime. One objective is to spot situations where the pattern removes large conditional logic blocks, such as choosing different shipping or discount calculations. Another goal is to evaluate how Strategy supports the Open/Closed Principle by allowing new algorithms to be added without modifying existing context code. Each objective includes a small mnemonic to help you remember the role of each component and a milestone indicating how to verify competency. For example, you should be able to implement a ShoppingCart that accepts DiscountStrategy implementations and demonstrate the cart applying different discounts at runtime. Finally, you will also learn when Strategy might be unnecessary and what simpler alternatives exist, so you can choose the right tool for the job.

These second objective cards focus on applying what you learn in code and verifying behavior. You should be able to implement concrete strategies that encapsulate different algorithms — for example, a percentage discount, a fixed amount discount, or no discount — and wire them into a ShoppingCart context. Practice toggling strategies at runtime and writing small, isolated tests for each strategy. Another objective is to judge when Strategy adds unnecessary complexity; for tiny variations a method parameter or factory method is often sufficient. Finally, be able to explain how Strategy differs from State: Strategy is chosen by the client to decide what algorithm to use, while State represents an object's internal condition that changes its behavior. These skills are practical: you will use them when you want modular algorithms and runtime flexibility without bloated conditional statements.

The Strategy pattern is a behavioral design pattern that defines a family of algorithms, encapsulates each algorithm in its own class, and makes them interchangeable within a context. In practical terms, the context delegates work to a strategy via a common interface and does not implement the algorithms itself. This separation keeps the context small and focused on coordination, while algorithm details live in dedicated classes that are easy to test. A concrete example is discount calculation: the ShoppingCart does not know how a particular discount is computed, it only asks its current DiscountStrategy to compute the final price. A key benefit is that you can add new strategies by creating new classes that implement the same interface, without changing the ShoppingCart; this supports the Open/Closed Principle. A common misconception is thinking Strategy is only about runtime swapping — while it enables that, its main value is encapsulation and clearer responsibilities. Consider a shipping calculation system: Strategy is ideal when multiple algorithms exist and you anticipate adding new ones or testing them in isolation. How would you design the interface for a task you need to swap?

Let's examine the three core components and how they interact in a Java implementation. The Strategy interface declares the operation the context will call, such as applyDiscount or calculateCost. ConcreteStrategy classes implement that interface and encapsulate a specific algorithm; for example, NoDiscountStrategy returns the original price, PercentageDiscountStrategy reduces the price by a percentage, and FixedAmountDiscountStrategy subtracts a fixed amount. The Context, such as ShoppingCart, stores a reference to a Strategy and delegates execution to it. The Context may also provide a setter so clients can change the strategy at runtime. In practice this means the ShoppingCart's calculateFinalPrice method simply calls discountStrategy. applyDiscount(totalPrice) and returns the result. This separation reduces conditional branches in the Context and makes each algorithm independently testable. A common implementation pitfall is letting the Context inspect the type of strategy or use instanceof checks—this defeats the pattern. Instead, code to the Strategy interface and let the ConcreteStrategy implement the details. As you design these parts, also think about default strategies and how to inject them safely to avoid null references. Core components: Context, Strategy, ConcreteStrategy means strategy = interface; concretestrategy = algorithm implementation; context = delegates to strategy and supports runtime swapping.. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

A frequent motivation for Strategy is replacing large conditional statements inside a class. Imagine a method filled with if-else branches to select multiple algorithms for shipping or discount calculations. Such code becomes brittle: adding a new algorithm requires editing the method, risking regressions and violating the Single Responsibility Principle. With Strategy, each algorithm is a separate class and the Context simply selects an instance to use. This yields several practical benefits: you can add a new ConcreteStrategy class without modifying the Context; unit tests can target each algorithm in isolation; and the Context logic stays short and readable. A common misunderstanding is that Strategy forces runtime selection. While it enables runtime choice, you can also choose a strategy once during construction and keep the Context unchanged afterwards. Another alternative is a factory method if the choice is made once at creation time. Use Strategy when algorithms form a family and you need flexibility or easier testing. Ask yourself: will algorithms likely grow or change? If yes, Strategy is a strong fit. NoDiscountStrategy returns the original amount. Here we make the practical case for using the Strategy pattern. The core claim is simple: when you move algorithmic variations into their own classes, your system becomes open for extension but closed for modification. That means adding a new algorithm rarely requires touching the context class or existing strategies. For example, if a ShoppingCart already delegates discounts to a DiscountStrategy interface, adding a seasonal discount only requires a new concrete class, not edits to the cart. This reduces risk and regression bugs when you extend behavior. You also gain testability: each concrete strategy has a narrow responsibility and can be unit-tested in isolation with simple inputs and expected outputs, without wiring a full ShoppingCart or UI. Reusability improves because multiple contexts can reuse the same strategy implementations where the algorithm applies. A common misunderstanding is that Strategy is only about avoiding switch statements; it is more about encapsulating variation and giving clients a clean way to choose algorithms at runtime. Finally, be mindful of cohesion: keep strategy classes focused and avoid moving unrelated responsibilities into them. Consider a quick reflective question: when you add a new algorithm, does any existing class change? If yes, Strategy might not yet be implemented correctly.

Strategy is powerful, but it is not always the simplest solution. The key question to ask is: how many algorithms are there, and how likely are they to change or grow? If you have one algorithm with a small boolean variation, a method parameter is often clearer and faster to implement. For example, a sort method with an ascending flag does not need a family of strategy classes. A Factory Method is a lightweight alternative when the choice of algorithm is decided once at creation time and does not change at runtime — the factory returns the correct concrete object and the rest of the system uses it without switching strategies later.
